title: Geometric-fibre hypotheses and fixed-pair transport for a given comparison system
statement:
Fix a finite-field datum $(p,a,q,k_0,k)$ [def-weil-finite-field-fiber], a prime $\ell\ne p$, an algebraic closure $\Omega/\mathbf Q_\ell$, and a separated finite-type $k_0$-scheme $X_0$ [def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Put $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$ and $g_X=\operatorname{id}_{X_0}\times\operatorname{Spec}(\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ is geometric Frobenius [def-weil-frobenius-detailed]. Suppose a simultaneous coefficient/pullback datum $S$ [def-fd-pullback-comparison-datum] is given on all noetherian finite-dimensional schemes with $\ell$ invertible, in the sense of [lem-weil-pbc-integral-stratified-perfect-characterization]. Write $J_{W,E},J_W$ for its finite and common-stage coefficient equivalences and $b_{h,E}:J_{U,E}F^s_{h,E}\simeq F^p_{h,E}J_{T,E}$, $b_h:J_UF_h^s\simeq F_h^pJ_T$ for its comparisons, using the inverses if the datum records the reverse orientation. The operations are the actual framework and PBC completed pullbacks [def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom, def-weil-pbc-completed-pullback].
Then $X$ is noetherian and finite dimensional, and $\ell$ is a unit in every local ring of $X$. The map $g_X$ is a scheme automorphism, with no assumption of $k$-linearity. For $\Lambda=E$ at any finite stage or $\Lambda=\Omega$ at the common stage, put $J=J_{X,\Lambda}$, $F_s=F^s_{g_X,\Lambda}$, $F_p=F^p_{g_X,\Lambda}$ and $b=b_{g_X,\Lambda}$. The formula
$$(K,\theta:F_sK\xrightarrow{\sim}K)\longmapsto(JK,J(\theta)\circ b_K^{-1}),\qquad u\longmapsto J(u)$$
defines an equivalence from the framework Weil-pair category [def-weil-weil-sheaf-complex] to the category of pairs $(H,\psi:F_pH\simeq H)$ with arrows $v$ satisfying $v\psi=\psi'F_p(v)$. The Hom bijection is exactly the underlying Hom bijection of $J$ restricted to intertwining arrows. These equivalences commute with the finite-stage inclusions into the common-stage pair categories and with scalar extensions, using the specified comparisons in $S$.

proof.text: Apply separated finite-type base change to $X_0\to\operatorname{Spec}k_0$ and the field extension $k/k_0$. This gives $X$ separated and of finite type over $k$. Concretely, its finite affine cover has coordinate rings $A_i\otimes_{k_0}k$; the images $a_{ij}\otimes1$ of generators of $A_i/k_0$ still generate over $k$. Thus the finite-type hypothesis needed below is for $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, without requiring $k/k_0$ finite.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 10: finite-type geometric fibre

proof.text: The only ideals of the field $k$ are $0$ and $k$, so every ideal is finitely generated; its one affine chart makes $\operatorname{Spec}k$ Noetherian. Apply finite-type-over-Noetherian to the structure morphism from step 1: $X$ is Noetherian. Apply the finite-type-over-a-field dimension lemma with $K=k$ to the same morphism: $\dim X<\infty$. The empty scheme is allowed, with dimension $-\infty$; hence this also supplies a finite nonnegative dimension bound in that case.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 10: Noetherian and finite-dimensional hypotheses

proof.text: Since $\operatorname{char}k=p$ and $\ell\ne p$, the image of $\ell$ in $k$ has inverse $\ell^{-1}$. Their images under $k\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ still multiply to $1$, for every $x$. Thus $\ell$ is invertible on $X$. The Frobenius definition gives $g_X$ and its inverse $\operatorname{id}_{X_0}\times\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi_q)$. Their composites are identities because $\gamma\varphi_q=\varphi_q\gamma=1$. Consequently $g_X$ is an allowed scheme isomorphism for $S$; no $k$-linearity is used.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 10: invertibility and semilinear scheme automorphism

proof.text: At either a finite stage or the common stage, take from the given datum its equivalence $J:\mathcal C_s\simeq\mathcal C_p$ and comparison $b:JF_s\simeq F_pJ$ for $g_X$. Use the inverse comparison if necessary. Write $\psi_K=J(\theta_K)b_K^{-1}$. This is an isomorphism $F_pJK\to JK$, since both factors are isomorphisms. The framework pairs are exactly the fixed pairs of $F_s$ in the Weil-complex definition; the target pairs are the fixed pairs of $F_p$.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: define the transported objects

proof.text:
For $u:K\to K'$, naturality gives $F_p(Ju)b_K=b_{K'}J(F_su)$. Therefore
$$Ju\,\psi_K=\psi_{K'}F_p(Ju)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J(u\theta_K)=J(\theta_{K'}F_su)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\theta_K=\theta_{K'}F_su.$$
The first equivalence substitutes $\psi$ and cancels $b_K$; the second uses injectivity of the Hom map of the supplied equivalence $J$. Thus $u\mapsto Ju$ defines a functor on pairs, preserves identities and composition, and its map on each Hom is exactly the restriction of the given bijection for $J$. The reverse implication shows that its inverse Hom bijection also lands in intertwining arrows, so the pair functor is fully faithful.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: naturality and the restricted Hom bijection

proof.text: Given a target pair $(H,\psi)$, choose $K$ and an isomorphism $v:JK\simeq H$ using the essential surjectivity of the equivalence in the datum. Put $\psi_0=v^{-1}\psi F_p(v):F_pJK\simeq JK$. Lift $\psi_0b_K:JF_sK\simeq JK$ by the Hom bijection of $J$ to $\theta:F_sK\to K$, and lift its inverse to $t:K\to F_sK$. Applying $J$ to the two composites and using injectivity gives $t\theta=1$ and $\theta t=1$. Thus $\theta$ is a Weil isomorphism, its transported structure is $\psi_0$, and $v\psi_0=\psi F_p(v)$ makes $v$ an isomorphism of pairs. This proves essential surjectivity without assuming $H$ is literally $JK$.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: lift a structure and its inverse on an arbitrary target object

proof.text: Apply the fully-faithful/essentially-surjective criterion to the pair functor from steps 4–6. Its hypotheses are precisely the restricted Hom bijections of step 5 and the isomorphisms $v$ of step 6. All categories and functors involved may be placed in a common larger universe, so the criterion applies. It produces an equivalence with this very functor, and therefore with the required arrow map and Hom bijection.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: conclude equivalence

proof.text:
For a finite extension $E\subset L$, denote the two scalar functors by $T_s,T_p$, their supplied Frobenius comparisons by $r_s:T_sF_{s,E}\simeq F_{s,L}T_s$ and $r_p:T_pF_{p,E}\simeq F_{p,L}T_p$, and the coefficient comparison by $j:J_LT_s\simeq T_pJ_E$. These are the actual scalar functors and comparisons in $S$. Its mixed square, with $b$ oriented as in the statement, reads
$$r_{p,J_EK}\,T_p(b_{E,K})\,j_{F_{s,E}K}=F_{p,L}(j_K)\,b_{L,T_sK}\,J_L(r_{s,K}).$$
This is an assumption of the given compatible transformation, not an additional coherence assertion about scheme composition.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: spell out the supplied mixed scalar square

proof.text:
The structure on the scalar extension of $(K,\theta)$ is $T_s(\theta)r_{s,K}^{-1}$. Naturality of $j$ at $\theta$, followed by rearrangement of the equation in step 8, gives
$$\begin{aligned}
j_KJ_L(T_s(\theta)r_{s,K}^{-1})b_{L,T_sK}^{-1}
&=T_p(J_E\theta)j_{F_{s,E}K}J_L(r_{s,K}^{-1})b_{L,T_sK}^{-1}\\
&=T_p(J_E\theta b_{E,K}^{-1})r_{p,J_EK}^{-1}F_{p,L}(j_K).
\end{aligned}$$
This is exactly the intertwining condition for $j_K$ between the two scalar-extended transported pairs. On arrows its naturality is that of $j$. Hence $j$ lifts to the required natural isomorphism of pair functors; its inverse also intertwines by cancelling this equation.

source.place: Final sentence; old parent step 11: explicit scalar-compatibility calculation

proof.text: The same displayed calculation applies to a finite-stage inclusion $I_s:\mathcal C_{s,E}\to\mathcal C_s$ and $I_p:\mathcal C_{p,E}\to\mathcal C_p$: replace $T_s,T_p,J_L$ by $I_s,I_p,J_X$. Here $r_s,r_p$ are their specified pullback comparisons. The datum says the common-stage coefficient functor preserves the field label and that the component of its pullback comparison at a literal pair is the inclusion of the finite component. Thus the equation in step 8 for these substitutions is the specified finite-to-common comparison equation. Step 9 proves that the coefficient inclusion comparison is an isomorphism of Weil pairs, natural in arrows. This proves commutation with every finite-stage inclusion. The scalar cocycle and identity equations remain true after lifting: their underlying maps are the supplied ones, and arrows of pairs are equal exactly when their underlying arrows are equal.
